title: What is Nadi Pariksha? Pulse Diagnosis in Ayurveda — Method, Preparation & Limits
excerpt: What does a vaidya feel with three fingers on your wrist? Learn what Nadi Pariksha is, where the texts describe it, what it can and cannot tell, how to prepare before the examination, common myths, and when you should go straight to hospital instead of waiting for a pulse check.
content:
“The vaidya just held my pulse and described all my troubles” — you have surely heard people say this. Nadi Pariksha (pulse examination) is an old and important method of examination in Ayurveda, in which the vaidya places fingers on the wrist, feels the speed, strength, rhythm and character of the pulse (nadi), and from it tries to understand the state of the doshas in the body.

But Nadi Pariksha is not magic or a miracle, nor is it a substitute for modern tests. In this article we explain in simple language what it is, how it is done, how to prepare for it and what its limits are. This article is for information only — take any treatment only on the advice of your vaidya or doctor.

What is Nadi Pariksha?

Ayurveda describes many ways of examining a patient — looking, touching, asking and so on. In later texts the pulse is given first place in Ashtavidha Pariksha (the eightfold examination). Usually the vaidya places three fingers on the wrist near the root of the thumb, and according to tradition:

  • Under the index finger — the movement of Vata dosha is felt
  • Under the middle finger — the movement of Pitta dosha is felt
  • Under the ring finger — the movement of Kapha dosha is felt

Traditionally the right wrist is examined in men and the left in women, although experienced vaidyas often check both hands. The gait of the pulse is compared to the movements of a snake, a frog or a swan — understanding these needs years of practice and learning from a teacher.

Nadi Pariksha in the texts

The Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas do not describe pulse examination in detail; it is clearly described in later texts — such as the Sharngadhara Samhita, Yogaratnakara and Bhavaprakasha. The Sharngadhara Samhita says:

करस्याङ्गुष्ठमूले या धमनी जीवसाक्षिणी ।
तच्चेष्टया सुखं दुःखं ज्ञेयं कायस्य पण्डितैः ॥
— Sharngadhara Samhita, Purva Khanda, Chapter 3

Meaning: The artery (nadi) at the root of the thumb is the witness of life; from its movement the learned physician should know the well-being (health) and suffering (disease) of the body.

So the pulse is called the “witness of life” — it shows whether the body is in balance or out of balance. But the texts also say that the pulse should be understood only together with other examinations, such as the patient’s symptoms, history, tongue, stool and urine, eyes, voice and build. In Ayurveda, diagnosis is always made by “putting everything together”, not from the pulse alone.

What the pulse helps to understand

  • A sign of the person’s prakriti (inborn Vata-Pitta-Kapha nature)
  • Which doshas are increased or decreased at present — the vikriti (current imbalance)
  • The state of agni (digestion and metabolism) — weak, sharp or irregular
  • Signs of ama (undigested, heaviness-producing matter) in the body
  • An impression of general states such as tiredness, stress, restlessness or weakness
  • When checked repeatedly during treatment — the changes in the doshas, that is, the effect of treatment

Limits of Nadi Pariksha

  • It is not a substitute for BP, blood sugar, ECG, blood tests, X-ray or ultrasound
  • Conditions such as cancer, pregnancy, a fracture or an infection cannot be confirmed by the pulse
  • Reading it well depends on years of practice; opinions of different vaidyas can differ
  • Food, exercise, tea or coffee, fear, fever and some medicines change the pulse temporarily
  • Research on Nadi Pariksha in modern science is still limited
  • Claims like “we will name every disease just by feeling the pulse” are not trustworthy

That is why at our clinics Nadi Pariksha is read together with your test reports (such as CBC, sugar, thyroid, LFT/KFT, ultrasound) and the symptoms you describe. When needed, we also advise modern tests and a visit to a specialist doctor.

Preparing for Nadi Pariksha

The pulse shows the body’s state at that moment, so the right preparation makes the examination more useful. Traditionally it is considered best to check the pulse in the morning, on an empty stomach or a few hours after a light breakfast — this is why our OPD is held in the morning.

What to do

  • Come in the morning; if possible avoid a heavy meal for 2–3 hours before the examination
  • After arriving, sit calmly for 5–10 minutes and let your breathing settle
  • Bring all your test reports and old prescriptions
  • Keep a list of all current medicines, supplements and herbs
  • Do tell the vaidya about pregnancy, breastfeeding, recent surgery or any allergy
  • Remove a tight watch, bangle or thread from the wrist during the examination

What to avoid

  • A full meal, tea or coffee just before the examination
  • Rushing, climbing stairs quickly or coming straight after exercise
  • Bathing, oil massage or long sun exposure just before
  • Smoking, alcohol or tobacco — especially on the day of the examination

How the examination is done — step by step

  • The vaidya asks about your complaint, how long you have had it, your sleep, appetite, bowel and bladder habits and routine
  • You sit comfortably, with the hand relaxed and the elbow slightly bent
  • The vaidya feels the pulse for a few minutes with three fingers, applying different pressures
  • If needed, the other hand is also examined
  • The tongue, eyes, skin, voice and build are also observed
  • Then, after looking at your reports, your prakriti, vikriti and further treatment are discussed

Prakriti and vikriti — understand the difference

Prakriti is your inborn nature, which stays roughly the same throughout life — in some people Vata dominates, in some Pitta and in some Kapha. Vikriti is the imbalance that has arisen now because of wrong diet, routine, season, stress or disease. The aim of treatment is to correct the vikriti and bring the person back to the balance of their own prakriti — which is why two people with the same disease may be given different diets and treatments.

Common myths

  • “The pulse reveals the name of every disease” — no; the pulse indicates dosha imbalance, and other tests may be needed to confirm a disease
  • “If the pulse has been checked, reports are not needed” — wrong; together they make the full picture
  • “Change your medicines as soon as the pulse is checked” — never stop current medicines on your own
  • “One pulse check is enough” — checking again during treatment shows the changes

Nadi Pariksha is the art of an experienced hand — it cannot be fully replaced by an app, a watch or a machine giving a “pulse report”. A fitness watch only counts heartbeats; it does not show the state of the doshas.

Treatment after Nadi Pariksha — with caution

Combining the pulse examination, symptoms and reports, the vaidya advises you on diet and lifestyle guidance, yoga and pranayama and, if needed, medicines. After examination, when suitable, therapies done at the clinic — such as Marma therapy, Agnikarma, Jalauka (leech) therapy, cupping therapy, Nasya karma or Viddhakarma — may also be suggested. But:

  • Which medicine or therapy, in what dose and for how long — this is decided only after looking at the stage of the disease, age, prakriti, pulse, reports and current medicines.
  • Do not stop your current medicines (such as for BP, sugar, thyroid or the heart) on your own; make any change only on your doctor’s advice.
  • Give the vaidya full details of all your medicines and supplements so there is no clash; avoid “miracle medicines” without a name or address.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, any medicine or therapy only on the advice of a vaidya/doctor. Be wary of claims like “disease removed from the root with one pulse check”.

When not to wait for a pulse check — go straight to hospital

  • Chest pain, pressure or heaviness — especially with sweating or breathlessness
  • Sudden severe breathlessness or bluish lips
  • A drooping face, sudden weakness of an arm or leg, difficulty speaking — go to hospital immediately (signs of stroke)
  • High fever with confusion, unconsciousness or a stiff neck
  • Heavy bleeding, vomiting blood or black stools
  • Fainting, or a pulse that feels very fast, very slow or very irregular

Summary — points to remember

  • Nadi Pariksha is an important Ayurvedic examination that helps understand the doshas, agni and prakriti-vikriti
  • It does not replace modern tests — the two together are most useful
  • It is better to be examined in the morning, with a calm mind and some time after food or tea
  • Bring your reports and list of medicines; never stop current medicines on your own
  • With emergency symptoms do not wait for a pulse check — go straight to hospital
